source.text: וַיִּקְבְּצ֧וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֛ים אֶת־כָּל־מַחֲנֵיהֶ֖ם אֲפֵ֑קָה וְיִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל חֹנִ֔ים בַּעַ֖יִן אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּיִזְרְעֶֽאל׃

records.literal_gloss: And gathered [the] Philistines all their camps to Aphek, and Israel [were] encamping at the spring which [is] in Jezreel.

en.L: And the Philistines gathered all their camps to Aphek, and Israel was encamped by the spring that is in Jezreel.
en.B: The Philistines gathered all their forces at Aphek, while Israel was camped by the spring in Jezreel.
en.R: The Philistines brought all their armies together at Aphek. The Israelites were camped by the spring in the valley of Jezreel.

decisions.choice: the Philistines gathered: the story returns to 28:1-2
decisions.reason: Chapter 28 began with the Philistines gathering for war and Achish taking David with him (28:1-2). The account then turned to Saul at Endor (28:3-25). This verse picks up the Philistine march again, at an earlier point: the armies are still assembling at Aphek, before they reach Shunem and Jezreel (28:4; verse 11).

decisions.choice: Aphek and Jezreel: the Philistine gathering place and the Israelite camp
decisions.reason: This Aphek lies on the coastal plain, where the Philistine armies had gathered before (4:1). From there they marched north to the valley of Jezreel, where Israel camped by a spring below Mount Gilboa, the place of the battle in chapter 31 (31:1).

decisions.choice: camps: armies, the fighting forces
decisions.reason: The word means a camp, and also the troops that make up a camp. Here it is all the Philistine forces, each city's army with its own camp.

decisions.choice: The Israelites; the valley of Jezreel
decisions.reason: Readable names the people rather than the land, and says that Jezreel here is the valley, so that it is clear where the armies faced each other.

source.text: וְסַרְנֵ֤י פְלִשְׁתִּים֙ עֹֽבְרִ֔ים לְמֵא֖וֹת וְלַאֲלָפִ֑ים וְדָוִ֣ד וַאֲנָשָׁ֗יו עֹֽבְרִ֛ים בָּאַחֲרֹנָ֖ה עִם־אָכִֽישׁ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] rulers of [the] Philistines [were] passing on by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men [were] passing on in the rear with Achish.

en.L: And the rulers of the Philistines were passing on by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were passing on at the rear with Achish.
en.B: As the rulers of the Philistines marched past with their units of hundreds and thousands, David and his men were marching at the rear with Achish.
en.R: The Philistine rulers marched past with their troops in groups of a hundred and a thousand. David and his men marched at the back with Achish.

decisions.choice: the rulers of the Philistines: the lords of the five Philistine cities
decisions.reason: This is the title of the rulers of the five Philistine cities, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron (6:17-18). Achish is one of them, the king of Gath (27:2).

decisions.choice: passing on by hundreds and by thousands: marching past in their army units
decisions.reason: Each ruler leads his troops in units of a hundred and a thousand as they pass by, perhaps in review before the battle. This is how the commanders see David's band among them.

decisions.choice: in the rear with Achish: as Achish's own guard
decisions.reason: Achish had made David his bodyguard for life (28:2), so David and his men march with the king of Gath at the back of the column.

decisions.choice: with their units (Balanced); with their troops in groups (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "by hundreds and by thousands". Balanced and Readable say that these are the units of soldiers each ruler leads.

source.text: וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ שָׂרֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים מָ֖ה הָעִבְרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אָכִ֜ישׁ אֶל־שָׂרֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֗ים הֲלֽוֹא־זֶ֨ה דָוִ֜ד עֶ֣בֶד׀שָׁא֣וּל מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָיָ֤ה אִתִּי֙ זֶ֤ה יָמִים֙ אוֹ־זֶ֣ה שָׁנִ֔ים וְלֹֽא־מָצָ֤אתִי בוֹ֙ מְא֔וּמָה מִיּ֥וֹם נָפְל֖וֹ עַד־הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] commanders of [the] Philistines, What [are] the Hebrews the these? And said Achish to [the] commanders of [the] Philistines, [Is] not this David, servant of Saul king of Israel, who has been with me this days or this years, and not I have found in him anything from [the] day of his falling until the day the this.

en.L: And the commanders of the Philistines said, "What are these Hebrews?" And Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul king of Israel, who has been with me these days or these years? And I have not found anything in him from the day he fell [to me] until this day."
en.B: The Philistine commanders asked, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish answered the commanders of the Philistines, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul king of Israel? He has been with me for some time now, a year or more, and from the day he came over to me until today I have found no fault in him."
en.R: The Philistine commanders asked, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish answered them, "This is David. He used to serve Saul, the king of Israel. He has been with me for more than a year. Ever since he came over to my side, I have not found anything wrong with him."

decisions.choice: commanders of the Philistines: the army's officers
decisions.reason: These are the military commanders, a different word from the "rulers" of the five cities in verse 2. In verse 6 Achish says it is the rulers who do not approve of David; the commanders speak for them.

decisions.choice: Hebrews: the name others used for Israelites
decisions.reason: Foreigners, and Philistines above all, call Israelites "Hebrews" (4:6; 13:19; 14:11). The question is scornful: what are these men doing in a Philistine army?

decisions.choice: these days or these years: for a long time now
decisions.reason: The phrase means a good while, perhaps more than a year. By the end of his stay David had lived in Philistine country a year and four months (27:7).

decisions.choice: the day he fell: the day he deserted to me
decisions.reason: To "fall" to someone means to go over to his side, to desert (2 Kings 25:11; Jeremiah 37:13-14). Achish counts David as a deserter from Saul whom he can trust (27:12).

decisions.choice: the servant of Saul (Literal, Balanced); used to serve Saul (Readable)
decisions.reason: Here the word means a king's officer, not a slave, so "servant" is used at every level, as for other officials of a king. Readable says it as an action, which makes plain that David no longer serves Saul.

source.text: וַיִּקְצְפ֨וּ עָלָ֜יו שָׂרֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֗ים וַיֹּ֣אמְרוּ לוֹ֩ שָׂרֵ֨י פְלִשְׁתִּ֜ים הָשֵׁ֣ב אֶת־הָאִ֗ישׁ וְיָשֹׁב֙ אֶל־מְקוֹמוֹ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הִפְקַדְתּ֣וֹ שָׁ֔ם וְלֹֽא־יֵרֵ֤ד עִמָּ֨נוּ֙ בַּמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וְלֹא־יִֽהְיֶה־לָּ֥נוּ לְשָׂטָ֖ן בַּמִּלְחָמָ֑ה וּבַמֶּ֗ה יִתְרַצֶּ֥ה זֶה֙ אֶל־אֲדֹנָ֔יו הֲל֕וֹא בְּרָאשֵׁ֖י הָאֲנָשִׁ֥ים הָהֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And were angry with him [the] commanders of [the] Philistines, and said to him [the] commanders of [the] Philistines, Send back the man, and let him return to his place where you assigned him there, and not he shall go down with us into the battle, and not he shall become to us as an adversary in the battle; and with what will make himself acceptable this one to his lord? [Is it] not with [the] heads of the men the those?

en.L: But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him, and the commanders of the Philistines said to him, "Send the man back, and let him return to his place where you assigned him, and he shall not go down with us into the battle, so that he does not become an adversary to us in the battle. And with what would this one make himself acceptable to his lord? Is it not with the heads of those men?
en.B: But the Philistine commanders were angry with Achish and said to him, "Send the man back! Let him go back to the place where you stationed him. He is not to go down to battle with us, or he may turn against us once the fighting starts. How could this fellow win back his master's favor? Surely with the heads of the men here!
en.R: But the Philistine commanders were angry with Achish. They said, "Send this man back to the town you gave him. He must not go into battle with us. Once the fighting starts, he could turn against us. Is there a better way for him to get back into his master's good graces? He could kill our men and take their heads to him!

decisions.choice: his place where you assigned him: the town of Ziklag
decisions.reason: Achish had given David the town of Ziklag to live in (27:5-6). The commanders want him sent back there, out of the battle.

decisions.choice: an adversary: an opponent who turns against us
decisions.reason: The word names anyone who opposes another, here a soldier who changes sides in the middle of the fight (compare 2 Samuel 19:23; 1 Kings 11:14). Elsewhere the same word becomes the name of the Accuser, Satan (Job 1:6), but here it is a human enemy.

decisions.choice: with what would he make himself acceptable to his lord: how better to win back Saul's favor
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer the commanders give: David could make peace with his master Saul by bringing him the heads of Philistine soldiers, as he once brought Goliath's (17:54, 57) and the foreskins of a hundred Philistines (18:27).

decisions.choice: those men: our own men
decisions.reason: "Those men" are the Philistine soldiers around them. The commanders may avoid saying "our men" as one avoids naming a harm one fears for oneself.

decisions.choice: angry with Achish
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "with him". Balanced and Readable name Achish so that the reader does not think the commanders were speaking to David.

decisions.choice: He could kill our men and take their heads to him
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what the question about "the heads of those men" implies and turns it into a plain statement.

source.text: הֲלוֹא־זֶ֣ה דָוִ֔ד אֲשֶׁ֧ר יַעֲנוּ־ל֛וֹ בַּמְּחֹל֖וֹת לֵאמֹ֑ר הִכָּ֤ה שָׁאוּל֙ בַּֽאֲלָפָ֔יו וְדָוִ֖ד בְּרִבְבֹתָֽיו׃ס

records.literal_gloss: [Is] not this David of whom they sing to one another in the dances, saying, Struck down Saul his thousands, and David his ten thousands?

en.L: Is this not David, of whom they sing to one another in the dances, saying, \q 'Saul has struck down his thousands, \q and David his ten thousands'?"
en.B: Is this not the David they sang about to one another as they danced, \q 'Saul has struck down his thousands, \q and David his tens of thousands'?"
en.R: This is the same David the women sang about as they danced. They sang, \q 'Saul has killed his thousands, \q and David his tens of thousands.'"

decisions.choice: the women's song of 18:7
decisions.reason: This is the third time the song is quoted, in the same words as 18:7 and 21:12. Saul heard it as setting David above him (18:8); in Gath it had put David in danger (21:12-13); now it is the reason the Philistine commanders will not let him fight beside them.

decisions.choice: sing to one another: sang in turn, one group answering another
decisions.reason: The verb usually means "answer". Used of singing it means a song sung in parts, one group replying to another, as in 18:7.

decisions.choice: his thousands ... his ten thousands: the marginal spelling
decisions.reason: As in 21:12, the consonants written in the text spell the endings of these two words in a shorter way, and the reading noted by the scribes in the margin gives the usual plural form, as in 18:7. The meaning is the same either way.

decisions.choice: the song in the same words as 18:7, set in two lines
decisions.reason: The song keeps the wording it has at each level in 18:7 and 21:12, so the reader hears the same lines each time. Readable turns the question into a statement and names the women who sang (18:6-7), since "they" alone would be unclear.

source.text: וַיִּקְרָ֨א אָכִ֜ישׁ אֶל־דָּוִ֗ד וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵ֠לָיו חַי־יְהוָ֞ה כִּי־יָשָׁ֣ר אַתָּ֗ה וְט֣וֹב בְּ֠עֵינַי צֵאתְךָ֨וּבֹאֲךָ֤ אִתִּי֙ בַּֽמַּחֲנֶ֔ה כִּ֠י לֹֽא־מָצָ֤אתִֽי בְךָ֙ רָעָ֔ה מִיּ֛וֹם בֹּאֲךָ֥ אֵלַ֖י עַד־הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה וּבְעֵינֵ֥י הַסְּרָנִ֖ים לֹֽא־ט֥וֹב אָֽתָּה׃

records.literal_gloss: And called Achish to David and said to him, [By the] life [of] Yahweh, surely upright [are] you, and good in my eyes [is] your going out and your coming in with me in the camp, for not I have found in you evil from [the] day of your coming to me until the day the this; but in [the] eyes of the rulers not good [are] you.

en.L: And Achish called David and said to him, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, you are upright, and your going out and your coming in with me in the camp [is] good in my eyes, for I have not found evil in you from the day you came to me until this day. But in the eyes of the rulers you are not good.
en.B: So Achish called David and said to him, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, you have been honest, and I would be glad to have you march out and come back with me in the army. I have found nothing wrong in you from the day you came to me until today. But the rulers do not approve of you.
en.R: So Achish called for David. He said, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, you have been loyal to me. I would be glad to have you go into battle with me in my army. Since the day you came to me, I have not found anything wrong with you. But the other rulers do not trust you.

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives: a Philistine king swears by Israel's God
decisions.reason: Achish swears by the life of Yahweh, the strongest oath an Israelite could make (20:3). He may use David's own oath to assure him that he means what he says. The narrator does not explain it.

decisions.choice: upright: straight, honest and loyal
decisions.reason: The word describes someone straight in his dealings. Achish trusts David completely, though the reader knows David had deceived him about his raids (27:8-12).

decisions.choice: your going out and your coming in: taking part in the campaign
decisions.reason: Going out and coming in is a common way to speak of leading or serving in war (18:13, 16; 2 Samuel 3:25). Achish would gladly have David fight beside him.

decisions.choice: in the eyes of the rulers you are not good: the rulers do not approve of you
decisions.reason: "Good in someone's eyes" means approved or pleasing to him. Achish sets his own view against the other rulers': to him David is good; to them he is not.

decisions.choice: honest (Balanced); loyal, do not trust you (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the Hebrew "upright" and "not good in their eyes" in everyday words. Readable adds "other" before rulers, since Achish is one of them.

source.text: וְעַתָּ֥ה שׁ֖וּב וְלֵ֣ךְ בְּשָׁל֑וֹם וְלֹֽא־תַעֲשֶׂ֣ה רָ֔ע בְּעֵינֵ֖י סַרְנֵ֥י פְלִשְׁתִּֽים׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And now return and go in peace, and not you shall do evil in [the] eyes of [the] rulers of [the] Philistines.

en.L: And now, return and go in peace, and do not do evil in the eyes of the rulers of the Philistines."
en.B: So now, go back, and go in peace. Do nothing to displease the rulers of the Philistines."
en.R: So go back now, and go in peace. Do not do anything that would upset the Philistine rulers."

decisions.choice: go in peace: a kind farewell
decisions.reason: "Go in peace" sends someone away with goodwill and a wish for his safety (1:17; 20:42). Achish dismisses David as a friend.

decisions.choice: do evil in the eyes of the rulers: do anything they would dislike
decisions.reason: To do evil in someone's eyes means to do what displeases him. Achish asks David not to provoke the rulers by staying or protesting.

decisions.choice: Do nothing to displease (Balanced); Do not do anything that would upset (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom, since "do evil" could sound as if Achish feared some crime.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֜ד אֶל־אָכִ֗ישׁ כִּ֣י מֶ֤ה עָשִׂ֨יתִי֙ וּמַה־מָּצָ֣אתָ בְעַבְדְּךָ֔ מִיּוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיִ֣יתִי לְפָנֶ֔יךָ עַ֖ד הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה כִּ֣י לֹ֤א אָבוֹא֙ וְנִלְחַ֔מְתִּי בְּאֹיְבֵ֖י אֲדֹנִ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said David to Achish, But what have I done? And what have you found in your servant from [the] day that I was before you until the day the this, that not I may go and fight against [the] enemies of my lord the king?

en.L: And David said to Achish, "But what have I done? And what have you found in your servant from the day that I was before you until this day, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?"
en.B: David said to Achish, "But what have I done? What fault have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go out and fight the enemies of my lord the king?"
en.R: David asked Achish, "What have I done wrong? Since the day I started serving you, what have you found against me? Why can I not go out and fight the enemies of my lord the king?"

decisions.choice: the enemies of my lord the king: words with a double edge
alternatives: my lord the king = Achish only
decisions.reason: On the surface David means Achish, and asks to fight Achish's enemies, the Israelites. But "my lord the king" is how David has spoken of Saul (24:9; 26:17), and the enemies of Saul would be the Philistines. The narrator leaves it open whom David truly means and what he would have done in the battle.

decisions.choice: from the day that I was before you: from the day I entered your service
decisions.reason: To "be before" a king is to stand in his presence as his servant (16:21-22).

decisions.choice: your servant: a polite way of saying "I"
decisions.reason: Speaking to a king, a subject calls himself "your servant" (17:32; 26:18).

decisions.choice: me
decisions.reason: Readable says "me" for the polite "your servant", which is how a reader today would say it. It keeps "my lord the king" so that the double meaning stays.

source.text: וַיַּ֣עַן אָכִישׁ֮ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל־דָּוִד֒ יָדַ֕עְתִּי כִּ֣י ט֥וֹב אַתָּ֛ה בְּעֵינַ֖י כְּמַלְאַ֣ךְ אֱלֹהִ֑ים אַ֣ךְ שָׂרֵ֤י פְלִשְׁתִּים֙ אָֽמְר֔וּ לֹֽא־יַעֲלֶ֥ה עִמָּ֖נוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And answered Achish and said to David, I know that good [are] you in my eyes like an angel of God; nevertheless [the] commanders of [the] Philistines have said, Not he shall go up with us into the battle.

en.L: And Achish answered and said to David, "I know that you are good in my eyes like an angel of God. Nevertheless the commanders of the Philistines have said, 'He shall not go up with us into the battle.'
en.B: Achish answered David, "I know that you are as good in my sight as an angel of God. But the Philistine commanders have said, 'He must not go up with us into battle.'
en.R: Achish answered David, "I know that you are as good as an angel from God, as far as I am concerned. But the Philistine commanders have said, 'He must not go into battle with us.'

decisions.choice: like an angel of God: wholly good and trustworthy
decisions.reason: To compare a man to an angel, a messenger from God, is high praise at a royal court: it says he is faultless and can be fully trusted. The same comparison is made of David later, for his wisdom and fairness as king (2 Samuel 14:17, 20; 19:28). On the lips of a Philistine the word for God could also be heard as "gods", making the phrase "a messenger of the gods", but Achish has just sworn by Yahweh (verse 6), so "God" fits his words here.

decisions.choice: nevertheless: yet, all the same
decisions.reason: The word sets Achish's own trust in David against the commanders' decision, which he cannot overrule.

decisions.choice: an angel of God (Literal, Balanced); an angel from God (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not mark the phrase as "the" angel, so "an angel" is used. Readable says "from God" to make plain that an angel is a messenger God sends.

decisions.choice: you are as good as an angel from God, as far as I am concerned
decisions.reason: Readable puts "in my eyes" at the end as "as far as I am concerned", so that the comparison comes first.

source.text: וְעַתָּה֙ הַשְׁכֵּ֣ם בַּבֹּ֔קֶר וְעַבְדֵ֥י אֲדֹנֶ֖יךָ אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֣אוּ אִתָּ֑ךְ וְהִשְׁכַּמְתֶּ֣ם בַּבֹּ֔קֶר וְא֥וֹר לָכֶ֖ם וָלֵֽכוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And now rise early in the morning, and [the] servants of your lord who came with you, and rise early in the morning, and [when] it is light for you, go.

en.L: And now, rise early in the morning, [you] and the servants of your lord who came with you. And rise early in the morning, and [when] it is light for you, go."
en.B: So get up early in the morning, you and your master's servants who came with you. Start early in the morning, and as soon as it is light, go."
en.R: So get up early in the morning, you and your master's men who came with you. Leave as soon as it is light."

decisions.choice: the servants of your lord: David's men, once subjects of Saul
decisions.reason: "Your lord" is most likely Saul. Achish describes David's men as Saul's subjects who came over to Gath with David, perhaps hinting why the commanders do not trust them. It could also be Achish's own polite way of speaking of himself, but nothing in the verse shows that.

decisions.choice: a shorter text
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation has a longer verse here: Achish also tells David to go to the place he had assigned him and not to let any bad thought stay in his heart, because he is good in Achish's sight. The Hebrew text, followed here, does not have these words. Reviewers should check the evidence.

decisions.choice: rise early ... rise early: the order repeated
decisions.reason: Achish says twice that they must start early. The repetition presses the point: David and his men must be gone before the armies march.

decisions.choice: one command to get up early, then Leave as soon as it is light
decisions.reason: Readable gives the repeated order once, since it adds no new meaning, and keeps the time of leaving.

decisions.choice: your master's men
decisions.reason: Readable uses "men" for the servants, who are David's fighting men (verse 2), not household servants.

source.text: וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם דָּוִ֜ד ה֤וּא וַֽאֲנָשָׁיו֙ לָלֶ֣כֶת בַּבֹּ֔קֶר לָשׁ֖וּב אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֖ים עָל֥וּ יִזְרְעֶֽאל׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And rose early David, he and his men, to go in the morning, to return to [the] land of [the] Philistines; and [the] Philistines went up [to] Jezreel.

en.L: And David rose early, he and his men, to go in the morning, to return to the land of the Philistines. And the Philistines went up [to] Jezreel.
en.B: So David and his men got up early to set out in the morning and go back to the land of the Philistines, while the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
en.R: So David and his men got up early in the morning and set out to go back to the land of the Philistines. And the Philistine army went up to Jezreel.

decisions.choice: the Philistines went up to Jezreel: the two parties go opposite ways
decisions.reason: The verse sets David's return south against the Philistines' march north to fight Israel. David is kept out of the battle in which Saul dies (31:1-6), and he goes back to find Ziklag raided (30:1).

decisions.choice: the land of the Philistines: back to Ziklag
decisions.reason: David returns to the town Achish gave him in Philistine territory (27:6; 30:1).

decisions.choice: the Philistine army
decisions.reason: Readable says "army" to show that it is the fighting force, not the whole people, that marches to Jezreel.
